qt: to the Commission Susana Solís Pérez (PPE) Subject:

Gijón is a port in the TEN-T core network and its rail access must meet the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2024/1679 for freight by 2030: 740 m trains, P400 gauge, electrification at 25 kV and equipped with the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS). However, the Oviedo-Gijón renovation project put out to tender by Spain’s state-owned rail enterprise Adif, as part of the Plan de Cercanías (‘Local Transport Plan’), is limited to extending the gauge, and not including the 740 m, electrification or ERTMS, and its excludes the access branches to the quay (lines 150, 152 and 144), implemented by the port authority using the Iberian gauge. In addition, the regulation set a deadline of 18 July 2026 for Member States to assess the core network lines eligible for migration to standard gauge (1 435 mm) or to justify their exclusion on the basis of a cost-benefit analysis. In view of the above: 1.

Has the Commission received the assessment submitted by Spain and does it include the Pola de Lena-Gijón axis? If not, does it have the cost-benefit analysis to justify not carrying out the migration?
Does the Commission believe that the Oviedo-Gijón project will meet the requirements of the core network by 2030?
What assurances does the Commission offer to ensure compliance and what consequences does it foresee if rail access to the port of Gijón does not meet these standards?
This question is supported by a Member other than the author: Borja Giménez Larraz (PPE).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.10.2026) Different track gauges hamper interoperability, cross-border connectivity and the integration of the Union rail system. By contrast, a fully interoperable track gauge network can foster greater competition, benefiting both passengers and the wider economy. Pursuant to article 17(1), the trans-European transport network (TEN-T) Regulation1 creates an obligation of compliance with the European track gauge standard only for the new railway lines. As regards the existing railway lines located on the European Transport Corridors, the Commission has officially received the Spanish track gauge migration assessment pursuant to article 17(3) of the TEN-T Regulation. Although no formal opinion is required and considering the importance of the integration and interoperability of the Union rail system, the Commission intends to analyse the assessment, together with both Coordinators for the Atlantic and Mediterranean Corridors, within the coming months. The Spanish assessment is owned by the Spanish authorities, and any request for access should therefore be addressed to them. Under the TEN-T Regulation, non-standard-gauge networks are classified as ‘isolated networks’ and are therefore not subject to certain standards and requirements of the TEN-T Regulation, including electrification, loading gauge, European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS) and the enabling the operation of freight trains with a train length of at least 740 meters. Although not required to do so, Spain generally strives to achieve equivalent standards across its network, and the technical status of the isolated network shall be provided in the next Work Plan of the European Coordinator for the Atlantic Corridor to be published this autumn 2026.
